 In 1990 the IRS Seized Almost Everything Willie Nelson Owned Over a $16.7 Million Tax Bill. His Way Out Was a $19.95 Album
 Danielle Liverance Tue, November 17, 2026 at 8:17 PM EST 4 min read Quick Read 
 The IRS seized Willie Nelson's ranch, studio and more on November 9, 1990, saying he owed $16.7 million in back taxes from disallowed tax shelters. 
 He and the IRS agreed on "The IRS Tapes," sold by phone for $19.95. It raised $3.6 million toward the debt; a settlement with Price Waterhouse covered the rest. 
 The IRS holds the taxpayer responsible even when an adviser set up the investment. Failure-to-pay penalties run 0.5% a month, up to 25%.

 On November 9, 1990, federal agents seized almost everything Willie Nelson owned. He was 57. 
 The IRS said the country singer owed $16.7 million in back taxes. Agents froze his bank accounts and took his ranch in Dripping Springs, Texas, his Pedernales recording studio and golf course, at least 20 other properties, and his memorabilia, recordings and instruments. 
 Natalia Bratslavsky / iStock via Getty Images They did not get his guitar, Trigger. His daughter Lana had shipped it to him in Hawaii before the raids. 
 How a star ends up owing $16.7 million 
 The bill grew out of tax shelters. In the 1980s Nelson put money into investments that let him take big deductions, and the federal government later ruled those shelters illegal. The deductions were disallowed, and the taxes, interest and penalties came due at once. Nelson's accountants at the time were Price Waterhouse. 
 His lawyers negotiated a $6 million cash settlement with the IRS. Nelson didn't have $6 million. 
 The album 
 So Nelson and the IRS agreed on something unusual: an album. "The IRS Tapes: Who'll Buy My Memories?" was a stripped-down record of Nelson and his guitar, sold by mail order starting in 1991 for $19.95 through a toll-free number. Nelson promoted it on ABC's "Primetime Live" wearing a T-shirt printed with 1-800-IRS-TAPE. The number didn't exist yet. After 500 calls, the man who held it offered it to him.

 The money was split among the IRS, Nelson, the promoter, Sony and the album's costs. It raised $3.6 million toward the debt. 
 Fans helped too. A farmers' lobbying group bought Nelson's 44-acre San Marcos ranch at the IRS sale to sell back to him. 
 Nelson also sued Price Waterhouse and settled. The settlement and his other income covered the rest of the bill. 
 What it means for your money 
 Nelson's story is an extreme version of a common one: a deduction someone else recommended gets thrown out, and the taxpayer owes the bill. The IRS holds the person who signs the return responsible, even when an adviser set up the investment. 
 Penalties keep running. The IRS failure-to-pay penalty is 0.5% of the unpaid tax for each month it stays unpaid, up to 25%, and interest is charged on top. 
 Payment plans exist. People who can't pay at once can ask the IRS for an installment agreement, or offer to settle for less through an offer in compromise, which the IRS accepts when it agrees you can't pay the full amount. 
 Too good to be true often is. The IRS publishes a yearly "Dirty Dozen" list of tax schemes, and abusive tax shelters are a regular entry.
